Marathon Petroleum's stock dropped 6.6% today, extending a two-week decline that has now erased earlier gains. The timing aligns directly with oil prices falling sharply on October 27th after Iran's supreme leader signaled openness to ending the U.S.-Israeli war—a major geopolitical de-escalation that immediately reduced the premium markets had been paying for Middle East supply risk. Refiners like Marathon profit most when crude oil prices are high and stable; when that risk premium evaporates, so does part of the stock's appeal.

The broader picture shows that for the past week, oil prices had been climbing on Middle East tensions (hitting a six-month high of $116 on October 23rd), which actually helped refiners by boosting margins. Now that diplomatic signals suggest those tensions may ease, the refining sector is facing a headwind—lower oil prices typically mean tighter margins and reduced profit potential for a company whose earnings depend on processing crude into fuel products at a profitable spread.
